learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge in basic and technological subjects, enabling them to learn new methods and theories, and providing them with versatility to adapt to new situations.
Knowledge of atomic structures and their defects and ability to control material properties by modifying atomic structures with defects.
Knowledge of the magnitudes that define the different properties characterizing the behavior of industrial materials.
Knowledge of phase diagrams enabling them to fluently handle binary equilibrium diagrams and the fundamentals of ternary diagrams.
Knowledge of the fundamentals of materials science, technology, and chemistry. Understand the relationship between microstructure, synthesis or processing, and the properties of metallic materials.
Ability to design heat treatments to modify the microstructure and properties of steels, cast irons, and non-ferrous alloys.
Ability to use diverse materials and join them appropriately to design composite materials with controlled properties.
Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity, and critical reasoning.
Basic knowledge of concepts related to product verification and inspection and ability to handle specifications, regulations, and mandatory standards.
Identify the structures of fundamental crystalline solids and assess the importance of different structural defects.
Interpret the different properties of materials and also be able to determine them experimentally using appropriate testing techniques.
Interpret equilibrium diagrams and use them in material development.

Fluently handle the Fe-C diagram, transformation curves, evaluate the influence of alloying elements in these products, the practical use of Jominy hardenability curves of steels, and the effects of heat treatments.
Discern the main characteristics of industrially relevant non-ferrous alloys that justify their application, assess the importance of alloying elements and the effects of heat treatments.
Differentiate between the different families of plastic materials, ceramics, and composite materials, their main characteristics, advantages, and limitations for industrial use.
Ability to define the fundamental characteristics that describe crystalline structures.
Ability to use diffusion laws for various calculations.
Ability to determine the conventional mechanical properties of industrial materials by performing corresponding experimental tests.
Ability to determine electrical, magnetic, thermal, and optical properties using experimental methods.
Ability to interpret binary equilibrium diagrams and to place points and determine the phases present in ternary diagrams.
Ability to interpret the Fe-C diagram and the transformation curves of steels and cast irons to modify their microstructure and properties through mechanical and thermal treatments.
Ability to prepare metallographic samples, perform heat treatments, and interpret the microstructures of iron-based materials.
Ability to interpret the basic equilibrium diagrams of the most important non-ferrous metallic alloys and use them to define their characteristic heat treatments.
Ability to handle and interpret equilibrium diagrams in ceramic systems and to control their properties from their manufacturing processes.
Ability to interpret the mechanical properties of plastics based on their structural characteristics and manufacturing processes.
Ability to calculate the properties of composite materials from those of their constituent simple materials.
Promote in the student a desire for the acquisition of scientific knowledge.
Lay the foundations for the student to be able to apply acquired knowledge in engineering.
Formation of an open, critical, and entrepreneurial spirit.

syllabus_topics: Crystallography. Metallographic preparation and determination of grain size.
Microstructures of steels and cast irons.
assessment_rules: For continuous assessment, the final grade is calculated as (P1+...+P5) + L + 0.65*EF, where P1...P5 are partial exams (max 3 points), L is laboratory note (max 0.5 points), and EF is the final exam (max 6.5 points). A minimum grade of 4 out of 10 in the final exam is required, with at least 30% of the value for each of its three parts, and the overall global grade must be 5 or higher to pass. For non-continuous assessment, a final exam covering the entire course is taken, consisting of a laboratory part (1 point) and a theory/exercises part (9 points). A minimum grade of 5 is required to pass, with at least 30% of the value for each of the three parts. Students who do not pass through continuous assessment can take extraordinary exams following traditional assessment criteria.
